slides.title: Smooth curves: clip and notch your seams
slides.subtitle: The small snip that turns lumpy necklines and puckered curves into crisp, flat edges.

slides.title: Why curves need help
slides.body: When you turn a curved seam, the seam allowance has to stretch or squash to fit. Without a little help it pulls and bunches, so the edge never lies flat.

slides.title: Clip inward curves
slides.body: On a concave curve, like a neckline, cut small straight slits into the seam allowance. They open up when you turn it, so the edge can spread smoothly.

slides.title: Notch outward curves
slides.body: On a convex curve, like a rounded collar, cut out tiny V shapes. Removing that extra fabric stops bulky ridges. Always stop just short of your stitching line.

slides.title: Save this for sewing day
slides.body: Our step-by-step instructions tell you exactly when to clip and when to notch.

posts.caption_ig:
Lumpy neckline? Puckered curve? The fix takes about 30 seconds and a pair of sharp scissors ✂️

Swipe to learn when to clip and when to notch: slits for inward curves, little V shapes for outward curves.

Golden rule: never cut through your stitching line!

Save this for your next neckline or collar 🪡

posts.topic: Do a stretch test before choosing a knit fabric

slides.title: Do a stretch test before buying knit fabric
slides.body: Hold 10 cm of knit against a ruler and gently stretch it. If it reaches 15 cm, that's 50% stretch. Check your pattern's recommendation first.

posts.caption_ig:
Not all knits are created equal, and the wrong stretch can ruin the fit 📏

Try this quick test: hold 10 cm of fabric against a ruler and gently pull. Reaches 15 cm? That's 50% stretch.

Check what your pattern recommends, then pick a knit that matches. Too little stretch feels tight, too much can grow and sag.

Did you know this trick? Tell us below 👇

posts.topic: Checking sleeve fit: upper arm width and sleeve length

slides.title: Sleeves that fit: 3 quick checks
slides.subtitle: Tight upper arms or sleeves that stop short? Check these before you cut your fabric.

slides.title: Measure your upper arm
slides.body: Measure around the fullest part of your upper arm. Then measure the sleeve pattern across the underarm. The sleeve should be a few centimetres wider for comfort.

slides.title: Check the sleeve length
slides.body: Measure from your shoulder point to your wrist with your elbow slightly bent. Compare it with the sleeve pattern and use its adjustment lines to lengthen or shorten.

slides.title: Add width evenly
slides.body: Need more room? Add half the extra width to each side of the sleeve seam at the underarm, then taper smoothly back to your size at the wrist.

slides.title: Find your perfect fit
slides.body: Every pattern includes sizes XS–XL with US and UK sizing and a clear size chart.

posts.caption_ig:
